description: We are "Northern Farmers' Future", farmers and innovators from Northern Uganda, where erratic rain, droughts and post-harvest losses hit smallholder farmers hard.Vision: climatesmart, food-secure farming communities. Mission: turn NASA rainfall, soil moisture and temperature data into simple planting and storage advice for farmers. Goals: better yields, less crop loss, stronger climate resilience. We bring farming and building skills; we need coders,  software developers, and many more.Join us!
summary:
Northern Farmers' Future (NFF) is a farm planning platform developed to help smallholder farmers in Northern Uganda make better decisions using NASA Earth observation data. The system combines rainfall, soil moisture, temperature and sunlight information with farmers' soil observations and crop history to recommend suitable crops and three-season crop rotations.

Beyond planting decisions, NFF helps farmers prepare for rainfall, harvest and store water, manage farming during dry seasons using locally developed greenhouses, and plan crop drying using portable solar dryers. It also incorporates AI-assisted crop photo analysis to identify possible pests, diseases and nutrient deficiencies and provide guidance on safer management practices.

Designed for rural accessibility, the platform supports smartphones, offline access to saved information, SMS, USSD and voice communication in English and local languages.

A working prototype was developed during the hackathon. The team proposes an initial pilot with 20–30 farmers in Otuke and Lira districts to evaluate the accuracy, usefulness and practical impact of the system.

Northern Farmers' Future -NFF Rotate

Project: Northern Farmers' Future (NFF)

Challenge: Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data

Pilot Area: Otuke and Lira Districts, Northern Uganda (proposed). Long-term ambition: Uganda and East Africa, Africa and other planets like MARS.

Users: Smallholder farmers, farmer groups, youth groups, women’s groups, churches dealing in community activities like farming, youth, people with disabilities and women empowerment, NGOs dealing in agriculture, government agencies, and agricultural extension officers.

Ways to use it: Smartphone web app (works offline for saved advice), SMS, USSD and voice call.

Pilot: Working prototype built during the sprint. Farmer pilot is proposed, not yet done.

Team leader’s email address: Solomonogwang286@gmail.com

Team leader’s contact: +256787007444

Northern Farmers' Future is a farm planning tool for small farmers in Northern Uganda and East Africa. It answers the questions a farmer asks every season: What should I plant next? When will the rain come? When should I dry my harvest? What is wrong with my crop?

Our project work following the following steps;-

The farmer tells the system where the farm is, what was planted in the last two seasons, what the soil looks like, and what matters most: food, money, drought protection or soil recovery.

The system collects NASA data for that place: rainfall, soil moisture, temperature, sunshine and how green the plants are from satellite images.

It compares this with a list of about 15 local crops, such as maize, sorghum, finger millet, cassava, beans, groundnuts, soybean, cowpea, sweet potato, sunflower and simsim. For each crop we record how much water it needs, what it does to the soil, and how long it takes to grow.

.It gives the farmer a three-season rotation plan. For example: groundnuts first, then sorghum, then soybean.During the year it sends short messages. Examples: rain is likely in the next 5 to 24 hours, so prepare your tank; strong sun tomorrow, a good day to use the solar dryer; dry weeks ahead, use stored water in the greenhouse.

If a crop looks sick, the farmer takes a photo. The system suggests the most likely pest, disease or lack of nutrients, and gives a natural treatment that does not harm people, soil or water.

.All advice reaches the farmer by phone app, SMS, or voice message, in Luo/Acholi, Luganda, Swahili or English.

2. Benefits of our project to the farmers:-

. Better planning.Farmers know what to plant and when, instead of guessing.

Less crop loss. Early warnings about dry spells, rain, pests and disease help farmers act in time.

  • More water in the dry season. Farmers catch and store free rain, then use it for vegetables and nurseries when the rain stops.
  • Healthier soil. Rotating cereals and legumes puts nutrients back and breaks the cycle of pests.
  • Less spoilage. Farmers dry their produce on the right days, so less food rots.
  • Lower costs and a cleaner farm. Natural treatments use materials farmers already have, such as Neem, wood ash and compost.
  • Reach for everyone. A farmer with a basic phone and no internet can still get advice by SMS.

3. NORTHERN FARMERS' FUTURE INTENDED IMPACT:

Our first step is a small pilot in Otuke and Lira districts with 20 to 30 farmers. NOTE: Smallholder farmers, farmer groups, youth groups, women’s groups, churches dealing in community activities like farming, youth, people with disabilities and women empowerment, NGOs dealing in agriculture, government agencies, and agricultural extension officers are also our areas of implementation.

We will measure what matters:

  • How many rain alerts matched the real rain,
  • How many farmers stored water and used it in the dry season,
  • Changes in yield and crop loss,
  • Use of chemical pesticides,
  • Whether farmers keep using the tool.

If the pilot works, we will grow the project across Uganda and to other East African countries through community groups, local government and partner organizations. Our long-term aim is steadier harvests, healthier soil, less pesticide use and farming families who can cope better with climate change. This supports the global goals on zero hunger, responsible production, climate action and life on land.

4. TOOLS WE USED IN DEVELOPING OUR DEMO (PROJECT)

Software and data:

  • NASA POWER API (Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources)
  • World Bank crop calendar dataset for localized data
  • Python with FastAPI for the advice engine and alerts
  • A web app that works offline, built with React, with Leaflet maps
  • A small image model that can run on a phone for the crop photo check

Hardware:

  • Smartphones and basic phones for farmers
  • Laptops for building and testing the system
  • Greenhouses and solar dryers we have built before, which the system gives advice for
  • Optional low-cost tools at community points, such as a rain gauge, a tank level marker and a soil moisture sensor, to check the satellite data

5. CREATIVE PARTS OF OUR PROJECT:

  • It turns NASA data into a simple message a farmer can act on the same day, not only a seasonal report.
  • It covers the full farming cycle: catch the rain, store it, grow through the dry season, protect the crop, and dry the harvest.
  • It connects to real equipment that farmers can use: our greenhouses and solar dryers.
  • It works on basic phones, and on smartphones, with SMS and Voice Messages, so farmers without internet are not left out.
  • It uses only natural and biological treatments for pests and disease.
  • It uses local crops, local languages and farmer feedback, so the advice fits Northern Uganda and gets better over time.

6. FACTORS WE (THE TEAM) CONSIDERED:

  • Phones and internet. Many farmers have no smartphone or data, so we built SMS, voice and offline options.
  • Language and reading skills. Messages are short, simple and available in local languages, with voice and icons.
  • Cost. Farmers should not pay for expensive sensors or chemicals. Sensors are optional.
  • Accuracy. Satellite data gives good regional guidance but cannot promise rain at one exact village and hour. Our alerts say "likely" and we will test them against real rain during the pilot.
  • Safety of advice. A photo check gives a likely cause, not a guarantee. For serious cases, farmers are told to contact an extension officer. Treatments come with safe-use notes.
  • Seasons and crops. The system follows the two rainy seasons and the crops farmers already know.
  • Trust. We will start with respected local leaders and show results on real farms.
  • Privacy. We collect only the information needed and ask for the farmer's permission.
  • Long-term use. We plan to work with extension services, cooperatives and community groups so the tool continues after the pilot.

7. IMPORTANCE TO THE AGRICULTURAL SECTOR:

Farming is the main source of food and income for most families in Northern Uganda and across East Africa, and most of it is done by small farmers who depend on rain. When rain comes late, stops early or falls in heavy storms, crops fail and families go hungry.

Poor soil, pests and diseases make the problem worse, and much of the harvest is lost after picking because it is not dried or stored well.

Many farmers also have little access to experts, soil tests or reliable weather information. Northern Farmers' Future gives them practical advice at low cost, using free NASA data and simple tools. It helps farmers plan better, use water wisely, protect their soil and crops without harming the environment, and keep more of what they grow. This makes farming more reliable and more profitable, and helps rural communities handle climate change.

TEAM MEMBERS AND THEIR ROLES:

1. Ogwang Solomon, Team Lead and Innovator. Sets the direction of the project, designs the farm advice and the link to our greenhouses and solar dryers, works with farmers and partners, and leads the presentation.

2. Awongo Ducan, Software Developer (Front-end and Back-end Developer). Builds the app, the SMS service and the alert system, connects the NASA data, and develops the crop photo check (the client side and server side).

conclusion:

Farmers in Northern Uganda already know their land well. What many lack is timely information. Northern Farmers' Future brings NASA's view from space down to the farm in a form that any farmer can use: what to plant, when to prepare for rain, when to dry the harvest and how to treat a sick crop naturally. We will begin with a careful pilot, learn from the farmers, and improve the tool before sharing it across the region. We believe this can help farming families grow more food, protect their soil and water, and build a stronger future.
